# Axon guidance {#sec-guidance}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// Numbers used in the prose, computed from the cited values.
gdEphKolodkin = 8 + 6   // EphA + EphB receptors, Kolodkin & Tessier-Lavigne 2010, sec. "Ephrins"
gdEphrinKolodkin = 5 + 3 // ephrin-A + ephrin-B ligands, same section
```

Axons can grow "as much as several centimeters, or more than a thousand times the diameter of the cell body" to reach their targets [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124]. How does the growth cone (@sec-growth-cone) find its way? The classical answer is chemical: cells along the path display or secrete guidance cues, and receptors on the growth cone read them. A newer answer, from *Xenopus* embryos, is that tissue stiffness also steers axons. This chapter covers the chemical framework and ends with a short look at mechanics.

::: {.callout-note title="After this chapter you will be able to"}
- name the four guidance forces and give an example cue for each;
- match the four canonical cue families with their receptors and say whether each attracts or repels;
- explain how commissural axons cross the midline once and do not return;
- explain how calcium and cyclic nucleotides can switch a growth cone from attraction to repulsion.
:::

## Four guidance forces {#sec-guidance-forces}

A long trajectory is broken into short segments, "each perhaps a few hundred micrometers long" [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124]. Segments often end at **choice points** (intermediate targets): specialised cells that tell the axon where to go next. There, growth cones may slow down and grow more filopodia [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124].

Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman sorted guidance into four mechanisms: **contact attraction**, **chemoattraction**, **contact repulsion** and **chemorepulsion** [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1123]. "Contact" cues are bound to cells or matrix and act at short range; "chemo" cues are secreted and act at long range [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124, Fig. 1].

Note for anyone who coats culture dishes: "many adhesive substrates fail to support axon growth" [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124]. Repulsion, in turn, can deflect, stop or collapse a growth cone [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124].

The four forces act together. An axon may be "pushed" from behind by a chemorepellent, "pulled" by a chemoattractant and "hemmed in" by local cues (@fig-gd-forces) [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124]. Each decision reflects the balance of attraction and repulsion [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1130].

## Four families of cues {#sec-guidance-families}

Four families of cues are the best understood, each with its own receptors (@tbl-gd-cues) [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1959; @kolodkin2010mechanisms, sec. "Diversity of Guidance Cues for Developing Neuronal Processes"].

| Cue family | Receptors | Typical effect | Range | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Netrins | DCC family (attraction); UNC5 family (repulsion) | Bifunctional: attract some axons, repel others | Long (diffusing a few hundred µm in some settings) or short | @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Netrins"]; @tessierlavigne1996molecular [p. 1126] |
| Slits | Robo | Repulsion | Secreted; short-range at the fly midline | @dickson2002molecular [p. 1960]; @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Slits"] |
| Semaphorins | Plexins; for secreted class 3, neuropilin + plexin | Mostly repulsion; some can attract | Long and short | @dickson2002molecular [p. 1960]; @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Semaphorins"] |
| Ephrins | Eph receptors (ephrin-A binds EphA, ephrin-B binds EphB) | Attraction or repulsion; topographic maps | Short only | @dickson2002molecular [p. 1961]; @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Ephrins"] |

: The four canonical families of guidance cues and their receptors. {#tbl-gd-cues}

**Netrins** have attracted axons towards the midline "across more than 600 million years of evolution" [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1959]. In mouse embryos lacking netrin-1, commissural axons "give the appearance of wandering" [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1126].

**Slits** at the *Drosophila* midline stop axons from crossing, or from recrossing. Mice lacking Slit1 and Slit2 have no obvious spinal midline defects (Slit3 is still there) but striking defects at the optic chiasm, where retinal axons cross [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1960].

**Semaphorins** usually repel. Sema3A surrounds many peripheral nerves and keeps axons on track by "surround repulsion" [@kolodkin2010mechanisms, sec. "Semaphorins"]. Yet in the mammalian cortex Sema3A attracts the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons but repels their axons [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].

**Ephrins** must be clustered to activate their receptors, so they act only at short range [@kolodkin2010mechanisms, sec. "Ephrins"].

::: {.callout-important title="Where the reviews disagree"}
- **Size of the Sema domain** (the signature region of semaphorins): about 420 amino acids according to @dickson2002molecular [p. 1960]; about 500 according to @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Semaphorins"] and @tessierlavigne1996molecular [p. 1125].
- **Range of netrins**: "up to a few millimeters" in some cases according to @dickson2002molecular [p. 1959]; "a few hundred micrometers in some settings" according to @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Netrins"].
- **Number of Eph receptors and ephrins**: 13 receptors and 8 ephrins in mammals according to @dickson2002molecular [p. 1961]. @kolodkin2010mechanisms [sec. "Ephrins"] list 8 EphA + 6 EphB = ${gdEphKolodkin} receptors and 5 + 3 = ${gdEphrinKolodkin} ephrins, without naming a species.
:::

## Topographic maps {#sec-guidance-maps}

Ephrin-A ligands form a gradient across the tectum (the superior colliculus in mammals), and EphA receptors form a complementary gradient across the retina. Retinal axons with more EphA stop lower on the ephrin-A gradient, through repulsion [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1961]. When the ephrin-A gradient was removed in the mouse superior colliculus, retinal axons still filled the whole structure, but their order was disrupted. A second experiment, which raised EphA in half of the retinal axons, showed that mapping depends on an axon's EphA level relative to its neighbours, not on its absolute level [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1961].

## Switching at the midline {#sec-guidance-midline}

**Commissural axons** connect the two sides of the central nervous system. They grow to the midline, cross it once and never turn back [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963]. Before crossing, they are attracted by netrin and ignore the midline repellents Slit and certain class 3 semaphorins. After crossing, they ignore netrin (shown at least in the vertebrate hindbrain) and are repelled by Slit and semaphorins [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963, Fig. 3].

Slit silences netrin attraction through a direct interaction between Robo and DCC. In *Drosophila*, the protein Comm sends newly made Robo for degradation until the axon has crossed [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963]. In general, growth cones "extinguish their responses to certain cues and acquire responsiveness to others at key choice points" [@kolodkin2010mechanisms, Introduction].

## Inside the growth cone {#sec-guidance-signals}

Cues act on the cytoskeleton of @sec-growth-cone, through Rho GTPases among others [@kolodkin2010mechanisms, sec. "Guidance Cues and the Control of Cytoskeletal Dynamics"]. Filopodia may steer "by differential adhesion, generating mechanical force, or transducing distal signals" [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1961]. Forces do change: on immobilised netrin-1, growth cones of spinal commissural neurons increased their traction about tenfold, enough to redirect the axon [@franze2013mechanics, p. 240].

**Calcium.** In cultured *Xenopus* spinal neurons, turning towards netrin-1 needs Ca²⁺ influx and Ca²⁺ release from internal stores. A local Ca²⁺ rise, made by releasing caged Ca²⁺ with light, causes turning without netrin [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962]. In the *Xenopus* spinal cord in vivo, growth cones with frequent spontaneous Ca²⁺ transients (@sec-calcium) extended slowly; transients in filopodia regulate turning onto preferred substrates [@rosenberg2011calcium, sec. "Calcium-Mediated Regulation of Axon Outgrowth and Pathfinding"]. Dickson had judged evidence for a role in turning in vivo not yet "compelling" [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].

**Cyclic nucleotides.** Lowering cAMP or cGMP turns attraction into repulsion, and raising them turns repulsion into attraction [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962]. *Xenopus* retinal axons are attracted by netrin-1 at the exit of the eye and repelled by it at the tectum; these changes correlate with a gradual decline in cAMP and are reversed by raising cAMP [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962]. Timing matters too: cultured *Xenopus* neurons are repelled by netrin-1 early and attracted 8–10 h later, and blocking Ca²⁺ channels at late stages turns attraction back into repulsion [@moody2005ion, p. 906].

## Mechanical guidance, in brief {#sec-guidance-mechanics}

In *Xenopus*, retinal axons make a caudal turn in the brain "thought to be mainly controlled by the repellent chemical cues Slit1, Slit2 and Semaphorin3A" [@koser2016mechanosensing, PDF p. 2]. Three studies add mechanics:

- Stiffness maps of the living brain (stages 39–40) showed tissue stiffer in front of the tract than behind it. The axons turned towards the softer tissue, also on gradient gels without chemical cues [@koser2016mechanosensing, sec. "Axons grow towards soft tissue"]. This is the opposite of non-neuronal cells, which usually move towards stiffer substrates (**durotaxis**) [@koser2016mechanosensing, PDF p. 7].
- Live mapping (stages 33/34–37/38) showed the gradient appearing on average 18 min before the turn, and a gradient of at least (0.9 ± 0.4) Pa/µm was needed for axons to change direction [@thompson2019rapid, p. 3].
- Knocking down the mechanosensitive channel Piezo1 in the brain tissue around the axons lowered the expression of Slit1 and Sema3A [@pillai2026long, sec. "Piezo1 regulates expression of long-range guidance cues in vivo"].

Chemical and mechanical guidance are therefore linked. @sec-piezo introduces Piezo1, and @sec-frontier weighs this evidence.

## Check yourself {#sec-guidance-check}

**Match each cue with its receptor** [@kolodkin2010mechanisms; @dickson2002molecular]:

- Netrin-1, when it attracts commissural axons: {{< qselect "Robo|DCC|EphA|Neuropilin" correct=2 >}}
- Netrin, when it repels: {{< qselect "DCC|Robo|EphB|UNC5" correct=4 >}}
- Slit: {{< qselect "Robo|DCC|Plexin|EphA" correct=1 >}}
- Secreted class 3 semaphorins such as Sema3A: {{< qselect "Robo|DCC|Neuropilin and plexin|UNC5 with a DCC coreceptor" correct=3 >}}
- Ephrin-A in the tectum: {{< qselect "EphB|Robo|UNC5|EphA" correct=4 >}}

:::{.qmulti correct="3"}
A commissural axon has just crossed the floor plate. Why does it not turn back towards the netrin source?

- It no longer meets netrin, because the floor plate stops making it.

  > Netrin is still at the midline. What changes is the axon: after crossing it is insensitive to netrin [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963; Fig. 3].

- It is now attracted by Slit, which pulls it away from the midline.

  > Slit is a midline repellent. Commissural axons are repelled by Slit after crossing, not attracted [@dickson2002molecular, pp. 1960, 1963].

- It loses netrin attraction and gains Slit and semaphorin repulsion.

  > Correct [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963].

- It starts to destroy its Robo, so it ignores the midline Slit.

  > That is the state before crossing in *Drosophila*: Comm sends new Robo to lysosomes. After crossing, Comm is inactivated and Robo reaches the growth cone [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963].

:::

:::{.qmulti correct="2"}
A cultured *Xenopus* spinal neuron turns towards netrin-1. You lower cAMP inside the growth cone. What do you expect?

- It turns towards netrin-1 more strongly.

  > Raising cAMP favours attraction; lowering it converts attraction to repulsion [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].

- It turns away from netrin-1 instead of towards it.

  > Correct: lowering cAMP or cGMP converts attraction to repulsion [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].

- It still turns towards netrin-1, as cAMP acts on Sema3A responses.

  > Responses to netrin-1 depend on cAMP and PKA. It is the response to Sema3A that depends on cGMP and PKG [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].

- Its growth cone collapses and the axon retracts.

  > Collapse is a semaphorin effect: the first vertebrate semaphorin was purified as a potent inducer of sensory growth cone collapse [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1960]. Lowering cAMP changes the sign of the netrin-1 response: the growth cone turns away [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].

:::

:::{.qmulti correct="3"}
In the *Xenopus* optic tract, which way do retinal axons turn relative to a stiffness gradient?

- Towards the stiffer tissue, like most non-neuronal cells.

  > Non-neuronal cells usually migrate towards the stiffer side (durotaxis). Retinal axon bundles did the opposite [@koser2016mechanosensing, PDF p. 7].

- Towards the softer side in vitro, but the stiffer side in vivo.

  > The bundles turned towards the softer side both in vitro and in vivo [@koser2016mechanosensing, PDF p. 7].

- Towards the softer tissue, which lies caudal to the tract.

  > Correct. At stages 39–40, tissue rostral to the tract is stiffer than tissue caudal to it, and the axons turn towards the soft side [@koser2016mechanosensing, secs. "Stiffness gradients in developing brain tissue", "Axons grow towards soft tissue"].

- Towards the stiffer tissue, where axons extend faster.

  > Axons do extend faster on stiff gels (median 35.0 versus 22.6 µm/h), but the bundles turned towards the softer side [@koser2016mechanosensing, Fig. 1g; PDF p. 7].

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answers" collapse="true"}
1. Netrin attraction: DCC; netrin repulsion: UNC5; Slit: Robo; class 3 semaphorins: neuropilin with plexin; ephrin-A: EphA [@kolodkin2010mechanisms, secs. "Netrins", "Slits", "Semaphorins", "Ephrins"; @dickson2002molecular, pp. 1960–1961].
2. It loses netrin attraction and gains Slit and semaphorin repulsion [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963].
3. It turns away: lower cAMP converts attraction to repulsion [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962].
4. Towards the softer tissue, caudal to the tract [@koser2016mechanosensing, secs. "Stiffness gradients in developing brain tissue", "Axons grow towards soft tissue"].
:::

## Summary {#sec-guidance-summary}

- Growth cones are guided by contact attraction, chemoattraction, contact repulsion and chemorepulsion, acting together along short segments between choice points [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, pp. 1123–1124].
- The four canonical cue families and their receptors are netrins (DCC attracts, UNC5 repels), Slits (Robo), semaphorins (plexins, with neuropilins for class 3) and ephrins (Eph receptors) [@kolodkin2010mechanisms; @dickson2002molecular].
- Commissural axons cross the midline once because they switch from netrin attraction to Slit and semaphorin repulsion [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1963].
- Ca²⁺ signals and cAMP/cGMP levels inside the growth cone set whether a cue attracts or repels (cultured *Xenopus* neurons) [@dickson2002molecular, p. 1962; @moody2005ion, p. 906].
- In *Xenopus*, axons also turn towards softer tissue, and tissue mechanics regulates where chemical cues are made [@koser2016mechanosensing; @thompson2019rapid; @pillai2026long].

:::{.qflashcards}

- What are the four guidance forces?

  > Contact attraction, chemoattraction, contact repulsion and chemorepulsion.

- What does "bifunctional" mean for a guidance cue?

  > It attracts some axons and repels others, depending on the receptors they carry (netrin: DCC vs UNC5).

- Which receptor makes commissural axons sensitive to Slit after crossing?

  > Robo.

- What sets the position of a retinal axon in the tectum?

  > Its EphA level relative to its neighbours, read against an ephrin-A gradient.

- Which way do *Xenopus* retinal axons turn on a stiffness gradient?

  > Towards the softer side.

:::
